What is Cloud Computing: Cloud computing delivers computing services (servers, storage, databases, networking, software) over the internet. Key benefits: pay-as-you-go, elastic scaling, reduced maintenance, global reach.

# Cloud service models
# IaaS: Infrastructure (AWS EC2, GCP Compute)
# PaaS: Platform (Heroku, Google App Engine)
# SaaS: Software (Gmail, Office 365)
# FaaS: Functions (AWS Lambda, Cloud Functions)
Cloud Providers Overview: **AWS:** market leader, 200+ services. **Azure:** Microsoft ecosystem, enterprise focus. **GCP:** Google tools, data/AI strength. **DigitalOcean:** simple, developer-friendly. **Linode/Vultr:** budget options.

# AWS: aws.amazon.com
# Azure: azure.microsoft.com
# GCP: cloud.google.com
# DO: digitalocean.com
Regions & Availability Zones: **Regions** are geographic areas (us-east-1, eu-west-2). **Availability Zones (AZs)** are isolated data centers within a region. Deploy across multiple AZs for high availability. Choose regions close to users.

# AWS Regions
# us-east-1: N. Virginia
# eu-west-1: Ireland
# ap-southeast-1: Singapore
# Deploy in 3+ AZs for HA
Deployment Models: **Public cloud:** shared infrastructure (AWS, Azure, GCP). **Private cloud:** dedicated to one org. **Hybrid cloud:** mix of public and private. **Multi-cloud:** using multiple providers. **Community cloud:** shared by several orgs.

# Deployment comparison
# Public: scalable, cost-effective
# Private: secure, compliant
# Hybrid: best of both worlds
# Multi-cloud: avoid vendor lock-in

Virtual Machines (EC2): **AWS EC2** provides virtual servers. Choose instance types (general, compute, memory optimized). AMIs define OS/software. Security groups control traffic. Elastic IPs for static addresses.

# Launch EC2
aws ec2 run-instances 
  --image-id ami-xxxx 
  --instance-type t3.micro 
  --key-name my-key 
  --security-group-ids sg-xxx
Serverless (Lambda): **AWS Lambda** runs code without provisioning servers. Triggers: HTTP (API Gateway), S3 events, scheduled (CloudWatch), SQS. Supports Node.js, Python, Go, Java, C#, Ruby. Pay per execution + duration.
App Engine (GCP): **Google App Engine** is a PaaS that auto-scales apps. Standard environment (sandboxed, faster) vs Flexible (Docker, more features). Supports Go, Python, Java, Node.js, PHP, Ruby.

# app.yaml (GAE Standard)
 runtime: python312
 entrypoint: gunicorn -b :$PORT main:app
 automatic_scaling:
   min_instances: 1
   max_instances: 10
Containers (ECS/EKS): **ECS** (Elastic Container Service) runs Docker containers. **EKS** is managed Kubernetes. **Fargate** runs containers without managing servers. Use ECR for container image registry.

Object Storage (S3): **AWS S3** is object storage with 99.999999999% durability. Buckets hold objects. Storage classes: Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Glacier (archive). Versioning, lifecycle policies, static website hosting.

# S3 CLI
aws s3 mb s3://my-bucket
aws s3 cp file.txt s3://my-bucket/
aws s3 sync ./folder s3://my-bucket/folder
# Lifecycle rule (archive after 30d)
aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration ...
Block Storage (EBS): **EBS** provides block-level storage volumes for EC2. Types: gp3 (general), io2 (high-performance), st1 (throughput). Snapshots back up to S3. Can be encrypted. Attach to one instance at a time.

# Create EBS
aws ec2 create-volume \n  --volume-type gp3 \n  --size 100 \n  --availability-zone us-east-1a
# Snapshot
aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id vol-xxx
CDN (CloudFront): **CloudFront** is a CDN that caches content at edge locations. Origins: S3, HTTP server, ALB. Price classes determine edge coverage. Supports Lambda@Edge for custom logic at edge. SSL/TLS termination.

# CloudFront distribution
aws cloudfront create-distribution \n  --origin-domain-name my-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com \n  --default-root-object index.html
File Storage (EFS): **EFS** is a scalable, elastic NFS file system for Linux. Grows/shrinks automatically. Accessed by multiple EC2 instances simultaneously. Lifecycle management moves files to Infrequent Access tier.

# Mount EFS on EC2
sudo mount -t nfs4 \n  fs-xxxxx.efs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:/ /mnt/efs
# Automatic in fstab
fs-xxxxx.efs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:/ /mnt/efs nfs4 defaults,_netdev 0 0

RDS (Relational): **RDS** manages relational databases: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, Aurora. Features: Multi-AZ (HA), Read Replicas, automated backups, automated patching, encryption at rest.

# Create RDS MySQL
aws rds create-db-instance 
  --engine mysql 
  --db-instance-identifier mydb 
  --db-instance-class db.t3.micro 
  --master-username admin 
  --master-user-password secret 
  --allocated-storage 20
DynamoDB (NoSQL): **DynamoDB** is a fully managed NoSQL key-value and document database. Single-digit millisecond performance. Auto-scaling, DAX (caching), Global Tables (multi-region), On-Demand capacity.

# Create DynamoDB table
aws dynamodb create-table 
  --table-name Users 
  --attribute-definitions AttributeName=id,AttributeType=S 
  --key-schema AttributeName=id,KeyType=HASH 
  --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST
MongoDB Atlas: **MongoDB Atlas** is the official managed MongoDB service. Deploy across AWS/Azure/GCP. Features: auto-scaling, backups, BI Connector, Atlas Search, Serverless instances, global clusters.

# Atlas connection
mongosh "mongodb+srv://cluster.abcde.mongodb.net/"
# Create free cluster
# atlas clusters create --provider AWS --region US_EAST_1 --tier M0
Cloud SQL: **Cloud SQL** is GCP's managed relational database. Supports PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server. Features: automatic replication, backups, failover, encryption, private network access. Up to 30TB storage.

# Create Cloud SQL
gcloud sql instances create my-instance 
  --database-version POSTGRES_15 
  --tier db-f1-micro 
  --region us-central1 
  --root-password secret
Cosmos DB (Azure): **Cosmos DB** is Azure's globally distributed NoSQL database. Multi-model: document, key-value, graph, column-family. SLA-backed 99.999% availability. Single-digit ms latency anywhere in the world.

# Cosmos DB CLI
az cosmosdb create 
  --name my-cosmos-db 
  --resource-group my-rg 
  --kind GlobalDocumentDB
Firestore (GCP): **Firestore** is a flexible, scalable NoSQL database for mobile/web apps. Real-time updates via listeners. Automatic multi-region replication. Strong consistency. Serverless — no provisioning needed.

High Availability & Disaster Recovery: Multi-AZ: deploy across multiple availability zones in one region for resilience against AZ failure. Multi-region: deploy across geographic regions for region-level disaster recovery. RPO (Recovery Point Objective): max acceptable data loss (e.g., 1 hour = hourly backups). RTO (Recovery Time Objective): max acceptable downtime (e.g., 4 hours = time to restore). Backup strategies: automated snapshots, cross-region replication, point-in-time recovery. Failover patterns: Active-Passive (one region active, other on standby — Route53 failover), Active-Active (both regions serve traffic — Route53 latency routing, DynamoDB Global Tables, Cosmos DB multi-region writes). Common mistake: testing DR only once a year — automate DR drills. Use infrastructure as code to rebuild environments quickly.

# Multi-AZ RDS
# aws rds create-db-instance --multi-az --engine postgres --db-instance-identifier mydb

# Cross-region snapshot copy
# aws rds create-db-cluster-snapshot --db-cluster-identifier aurora-cluster
# aws rds copy-db-cluster-snapshot --source-db-cluster-snapshot-identifier arn:aws:rds:us-east-1:xxx:snapshot:xxx --target-db-cluster-snapshot-identifier my-snapshot-copy --destination-region us-west-2

# Route53 failover routing (active-passive DR)
# Create two records: primary (with health check) and secondary (with failover type)

# DynamoDB Global Tables (active-active multi-region)
# aws dynamodb create-global-table --global-table-name Orders --replication-group region-names us-east-1 us-west-2

# Azure Site Recovery (DR)
# az site-recovery vault create --name my-vault --resource-group my-rg --location eastus

# GCP: configure multi-region Cloud Storage
# gsutil mb -l US gs://my-bucket  # multi-region US

# Backup automation with lifecycle
# 1. Automated daily snapshot (retained 30 days)
# 2. Weekly snapshot (retained 3 months)
# 3. Monthly snapshot (retained 1 year)
# 4. Cross-region copy to DR region
Infrastructure as Code: IaC manages cloud resources through code (declarative or imperative). Terraform: multi-cloud, state management (local or remote like S3/Terraform Cloud), HCL syntax, modules for reusability. CloudFormation: AWS-native, YAML/JSON, StackSets for multi-account, drift detection. Pulumi: code in TypeScript, Python, Go, C# — full programming language power (loops, functions, conditionals). State management: store state remotely (S3 + DynamoDB locking for Terraform, Pulumi Cloud, CloudFormation managed by AWS). Modular design: break infrastructure into reusable modules (vpc, compute, database) with versioning. Common mistake: storing state locally or not using state locking. Never manually modify resources outside of IaC (drift). Use pre-commit hooks for formatting. Validate templates before apply.

# Terraform: module structure
# modules/
#   vpc/
#   compute/
#   database/
# environments/
#   dev/
#     main.tf
#     terraform.tfvars
#   prod/
#     main.tf
#     terraform.tfvars

# module "vpc" {

# Terraform commands

# terraform plan
# terraform apply -auto-approve
# terraform destroy

Cloud Security Best Practices: Shared Responsibility Model: provider secures the cloud (physical, network, hypervisor), you secure what's in the cloud (data, IAM, OS, app config). IAM least privilege: grant only required permissions — use service-specific roles, not admin. Encryption at rest: all cloud providers offer server-side encryption (SSE-S3, Azure SSE, GCP CSEK). Encryption in transit: enforce TLS 1.2+ everywhere, use HTTPS-only listeners. Secret management: store secrets in provider-native vaults (AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager) — never in code or config files. Common mistake: over-permissive IAM policies (using wildcards). Enable CloudTrail/Audit Logs and set up anomaly alerts. Rotate keys and credentials regularly. Enable MFA for all human users.

# IAM least privilege structure
# AWS: arn:aws:iam::xxx:policy/S3ReadOnly
# { Effect: Allow, Action: ['s3:GetObject'], Resource: 'arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/*' }

# Enforce TLS
# aws elbv2 create-listener --load-balancer-arn xxx --protocol HTTPS --port 443

# Secret retrieval at runtime (never hardcode)
# AWS: aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id prod/db/password
# Azure: az keyvault secret show --vault-name my-kv --name db-password
# GCP: gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret my-secret

# Enable audit logging
# aws cloudtrail create-trail --name my-trail --s3-bucket my-logs
# az monitor diagnostic-settings create --resource xxx --workspace my-logs
# gcloud logging buckets create my-bucket --location global

# KMS/CMEK for encryption at rest
# aws kms create-key --description 'app-key'
# az keyvault create --name my-kv
# gcloud kms keys create my-key --keyring my-keyring --location global --purpose encryption
Cost Optimization: Right-sizing: match instance size to workload needs — analyze utilization metrics and downsize over-provisioned resources. Reserved instances / Committed use discounts: 1yr or 3yr commitment saves 30-70% for predictable workloads. Spot/Preemptible instances: 60-90% discount for fault-tolerant, interruptible workloads (batch, ML training, CI/CD). Storage tiers: move infrequent data to cheaper tiers (S3 IA/Glacier, Azure Cool/Archive, GCP Nearline/Archive). Tagging strategy: tag all resources (Environment, Team, Project, Cost Center) for cost allocation and chargeback. Common mistake: leaving unused resources running (orphaned EBS volumes, idle load balancers, unattached IPs). Use budgets and alerts to track spending. Review and delete unused resources monthly.

# AWS: right-size EC2 with Compute Optimizer
# aws compute-optimizer get-ec2-instance-recommendations

# AWS: buy reserved instances
# aws ec2 purchase-reserved-instances-offering --offering-id xxx --instance-count 3

# Azure: reserved VM instances
# az reservation calculate --sku Standard_D2s_v3 --location eastus --quantity 3

# GCP: committed use discounts
# gcloud compute commitments create --region us-central1 --plan 12-month --resources vcpu=8,memory=32GB

# Tagging strategy
# aws ec2 create-tags --resources i-xxx --tags Key=Environment,Value=production Key=CostCenter,Value=123
# az tag create --resource-id /subscriptions/xxx --tags Environment=production CostCenter=123
# gcloud compute instances add-labels my-vm --labels=environment=production,cost-center=123

# Storage lifecycle (auto-tier to cheaper storage)
# AWS S3: transition to Glacier after 30 days
# Azure Blob: tier to Cool after 30 days
# GCS: set Nearline after 30 days

# Budget alert
# aws budgets create-budget ...
# az consumption budget create --amount 1000 --time-grain monthly
# gcloud billing budgets create --billing-account xxx --amount 1000 --currency USD
Microservices Architecture: Microservices decompose an app into small, independent services. Each service has its own database, API, and deployment pipeline. API Gateways (Kong, AWS API Gateway, Azure APIM, GCP Apigee) route requests, handle auth, rate limiting. Service mesh (Istio, Linkerd, Consul) manages service-to-service communication with mTLS, traffic splitting, observability. Circuit breakers (Resilience4j, Hystrix) prevent cascading failures — fail fast and degrade gracefully. Common mistake: premature decomposition — start with a monolith, extract services when needed. Anti-pattern: shared databases between services (tight coupling). Use eventual consistency and saga patterns for distributed transactions.

# Service decomposition example
# Monolith breaking into services:
# User Service - /users/* (PostgreSQL)
# Order Service - /orders/* (DynamoDB)
# Payment Service - /payments/* (RDS)
# Notification Service - async (SQS/SNS)

# API Gateway route (e.g., AWS)
# aws apigateway create-rest-api --name my-api
# aws apigateway create-resource --rest-api-id xxx --parent-id yyy --path-part orders

# Circuit breaker (pseudo-code)

# });
# const result = await circuitBreaker.call(request);

# Service mesh sidecar injection (K8s)

# istioctl install --set profile=demo

VPC (Virtual Private Cloud): **VPC** is a logically isolated network in AWS. Subnets divide IP ranges (public/private). Route tables direct traffic. Internet Gateway for public access. NAT Gateway for private subnets.

# Create VPC
aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16
aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id vpc-xxx --cidr-block 10.0.1.0/24
aws ec2 create-internet-gateway
aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --vpc-id vpc-xxx --internet-gateway-id igw-xxx
Load Balancers: **ALB** (Application LB) routes HTTP/HTTPS traffic. **NLB** (Network LB) handles TCP/UDP. **ELB** (Classic) is legacy. Target groups route to instances. Health checks detect failures. Auto Scaling integrates with LBs.

# Create ALB
aws elbv2 create-load-balancer 
  --name my-alb 
  --subnets subnet-xxx subnet-yyy 
  --security-groups sg-xxx
aws elbv2 create-target-group --name my-tg --protocol HTTP --port 80 --vpc-id vpc-xxx
IAM (Identity & Access): **IAM** manages users, groups, roles, and policies. Policies are JSON documents defining permissions (Allow/Deny). Least privilege principle. Roles for EC2/Lambda to access services. MFA for extra security.
Security Best Practices: Use IAM roles (not keys). Enable CloudTrail for auditing. Encrypt data at rest (KMS) and in transit (TLS). Security groups as firewalls. WAF for web attacks. Shield for DDoS. Regular security audits.

# Enable CloudTrail
aws cloudtrail create-trail --name my-trail --s3-bucket-name my-logs
# KMS encryption
aws kms create-key
aws s3api put-bucket-encryption --bucket my-bucket --server-side-encryption-configuration ...

Infrastructure as Code: Manage cloud resources with code. **Terraform:** multi-cloud, declarative HCL. **CloudFormation:** AWS-native JSON/YAML. **Pulumi:** code in Python/TS/Go. Version control your infrastructure!
Auto Scaling: **Auto Scaling** adjusts compute capacity based on demand. Launch template defines instance config. Scaling policies: target tracking, step scaling, scheduled. Health checks replace unhealthy instances.

# Create Auto Scaling group
aws autoscaling create-auto-scaling-group 
  --auto-scaling-group-name my-asg 
  --launch-template LaunchTemplateName=my-template 
  --min-size 2 --max-size 10 --desired-capacity 2 
  --vpc-zone-identifier subnet-xxx,subnet-yyy
CI/CD Pipelines: Automate build, test, deploy with CI/CD. **AWS CodePipeline** + CodeBuild + CodeDeploy. **GitHub Actions** for simpler workflows. **GitLab CI** with built-in registry. Test in staging before production.

# GitHub Actions workflow
name: Deploy
on: push to main
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm install && npm test
      - run: aws s3 sync ./dist s3://my-bucket
Monitoring & Logging: **CloudWatch:** metrics, logs, alarms. **X-Ray:** distributed tracing. **Prometheus + Grafana:** open-source monitoring. **ELK Stack:** Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana for log analysis. Set up alerts for critical metrics.

# CloudWatch alarm
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm 
  --alarm-name CPUHigh 
  --metric-name CPUUtilization 
  --namespace AWS/EC2 
  --threshold 80 --period 300 
  --evaluation-periods 2 
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:xxx

Multi-Cloud & Hybrid Strategies: Multi-cloud architectures distribute workloads across providers (AWS, Azure, GCP) for redundancy and cost optimization. Hybrid cloud connects on-premises infrastructure with public cloud via VPN or Direct Connect. Key patterns: cloud bursting (on-prem → cloud during spikes), data sovereignty (keep data in specific regions), and disaster recovery across clouds. Tools: Terraform for multi-cloud IaC, Cloudflare for multi-cloud networking. Challenges: data transfer costs, network latency, inconsistent APIs. Avoid vendor lock-in with Kubernetes, open-source databases, and provider-agnostic tooling.
Cloud Cost Optimization (FinOps): FinOps applies financial accountability to cloud spending. Key practices: right-sizing instances (matching capacity to demand), reserved instances (1-3 year commitments for 30-60% savings), spot instances (up to 90% discount for fault-tolerant workloads), auto-scaling (match capacity to demand), and storage tiering (hot/cold/archive). Tools: AWS Cost Explorer, Azure Cost Management, GCP Cloud Billing. Tag resources for cost allocation. Set budgets with alerts. Use savings plans for compute flexibility. Regular waste cleanup: delete unattached EBS volumes, idle load balancers, unused elastic IPs.
